$comment: L2 gloss layer for the ingested Missouri clauses: plain-language 'what this means' rewrites at two reading levels (src/schema/gloss.ts). Batch-drafted, then frozen; reviewed_by records the initial editorial pass — a named human reviewer should confirm each gloss against the clause text before classroom use. Reading levels are enforced by scripts/check-reading-level.mjs against READING_LEVEL_BANDS. A gloss explains only its own clause — it never imports rules from neighboring sections.

glosses.grade_5: The people keep two powers for themselves. They can write a new law and put it to a vote. They can also vote yes or no on a law the lawmakers passed.
glosses.grade_8: The people keep two powers. By initiative, they can propose a law or an amendment and pass it at the ballot. By referendum, they can approve or reject a law the general assembly passed.

glosses.grade_5: When a judge's job opens up, a special group picks three people who could do it. The governor must choose one of those three.
glosses.grade_8: When a judge's seat on certain courts opens up, a nonpartisan commission picks three candidates. The governor must appoint one of the three.

glosses.grade_5: You can vote in Missouri if you are a citizen of the United States, you are 18 or older, and you live here. The section also says when someone cannot vote.
glosses.grade_8: Voters must be United States citizens, at least eighteen, and residents of Missouri and their district. The section also lists times when a person cannot vote, such as while serving a felony sentence.

glosses.grade_5: Missouri says learning keeps people free. So the state must run free public schools that anyone up to age 21 can attend.
glosses.grade_8: An educated public protects everyone’s rights and freedom. So the constitution requires the state to establish and maintain free public schools, open to everyone up to age twenty-one.

glosses.grade_5: Everyone can follow their own faith, or none at all. The state cannot pick a church for you or punish your beliefs. Your beliefs do not let you break fair laws.
glosses.grade_8: Everyone may worship, or not, by their own conscience. The state cannot control belief or favor one faith. This liberty does not excuse acts that break laws protecting peace and safety.

glosses.grade_5: You are free to say and write what you think. No law can take that away. But you still answer for what you say.
glosses.grade_8: No law may limit free speech, in any form. Every person may speak, write, or publish their views. Each person still answers for abusing that liberty.

glosses.grade_5: People can gather in peace for a shared cause. They can also ask the state to fix something that is wrong.
glosses.grade_8: The people may gather peaceably for their common good. They may also petition the government to correct wrongs.

glosses.grade_5: The courts are open to every person. If someone harms you, you can ask a court for help. Justice cannot be sold or slowed on purpose.
glosses.grade_8: Courts must stay open to every person, with a remedy for every injury to person, property, or character. Justice may not be sold, denied, or delayed.

glosses.grade_5: The state's top power to carry out the laws belongs to the governor.
glosses.grade_8: The supreme executive power, the power to carry out the laws, belongs to the governor.

glosses.grade_5: The state's lawmakers can collect taxes for the state. Counties and towns can collect taxes too, if the lawmakers let them.
glosses.grade_8: The general assembly may tax for state purposes. Counties and other local governments may tax only under power the general assembly grants them.

glosses.grade_5: A change goes to the voters at the next big election. Each change is voted on by itself. If more than half the votes say yes, it starts thirty days later.
glosses.grade_8: Proposed amendments go on the ballot at the next general election, each voted on separately and each limited to one subject. If a majority of the votes cast on it say yes, it takes effect thirty days later.

glosses.grade_5: Missouri's lawmakers are two groups, not one. A bill must get a yes from both groups before it can be a law.
glosses.grade_8: Missouri vests its lawmaking power in two chambers, a senate and a house of representatives. Together they are called the General Assembly, and a bill has to pass both of them.
